questions.q: Why is best_score_ from a large grid search usually optimistic?
options: Cross-validation always inflates scores
It is computed on the training rows only
It is the maximum of many noisy scores, so it tends to include some luck
Grid search modifies the labels
questions.explain: Each candidate's score has random error. Choosing the highest of many tends to choose a lucky one, and reporting that score biases it upward.

questions.q: In the lesson, best_score_ was 0.75 while the average score over all 312 combinations was 0.672. What does the gap illustrate?
options: Most combinations are broken
Selecting the best from many candidates yields a flattering number
The test set was too small
Cross-validation failed
questions.explain: The search reports the top score from 312 tries. Its distance from the typical combination shows how much selection alone can add.

options: A hyperparameter search runs inside each fold of an outer cross-validation
Two test sets are averaged
Cross-validation is run twice with the same folds
The test set is used as an extra fold
questions.explain: Nested CV wraps the entire tuning procedure in an outer loop, so each outer fold is scored by a model whose tuning never saw it.

questions.q: In scikit-learn, what is a simple way to run nested cross-validation for a grid search?
options: Call gs.best_score_ twice
Pass the GridSearchCV object to cross_val_score with an outer cv
Set refit=False
Use train_test_split three times
questions.explain: cross_val_score(gs, X, y, cv=outer) refits the whole GridSearchCV inside every outer fold.

questions.q: After nested cross-validation has estimated performance, how do you build the final model?
options: Use the model from the best outer fold
Average the five outer models
You cannot build one after nested CV
Run a normal search on all the training data and fit the winner
questions.explain: Nested CV estimates how well the tuning procedure performs. The final model comes from running the search once on the full training data.
